DAILY METALS PULSE | SEPTEMBER 7, 2026

🥇 GOLD — JAPAN JUST SHOWED WHY GOLD IS MONEY

Japan spent dollars to defend the yen. Its gold defended Japan.

The headline figure is that Japan’s total reserves fell by a record $79.6B in August. But beneath the headline, its foreign-currency reserves actually declined by $94.6B, including an $87.8B reduction in its Treasury-heavy securities holdings.

Gold cushioned the damage.

Japan did not add a single ounce. Its holdings remained unchanged at 27.2M ounces, yet their value surged by $14.6B—from $109.5B to $124.1B.

Gold alone offset more than 15% of the foreign-currency reserve decline. Its share of Japan’s total reserves rose from 8.5% to 10.3% without Tokyo buying any additional metal.

That is the entire gold thesis demonstrated on the balance sheet of one of the world’s largest reserve holders:

• Dollars had to be spent.
• Foreign securities had to be sold.
• Gold simply sat there and became more valuable.

When monetary stress arrived, Japan’s interest-bearing paper assets were depleted while the supposedly “unproductive” asset strengthened the country’s balance sheet.

Gold is no one else’s liability. It cannot default, be sanctioned into worthlessness or be printed to defend a currency. Japan bought no additional gold in August, yet gold became dramatically more important to Japan.

Gold is nevertheless easing around $4,403 today after strong US employment data lifted the probability of a September Fed hike to roughly 58%. That is a short-term interest-rate headwind, with US PPI and CPI now this week’s major tests.

But Japan’s reserve report is the larger monetary story, and an exceptionally bullish advertisement for gold.

🥈 SILVER — LEVERAGE TO THE MONETARY TRADE

Silver is also down around 0.6% near $65.80 as higher-rate expectations pressure precious metals.

Silver does not enjoy gold’s central-bank reserve demand, but it offers greater leverage if concerns over currencies, sovereign debt and declining real purchasing power drive investors back into hard assets.

The physical market is still expected to record its sixth consecutive annual deficit in 2026. The projected 46.3Moz shortfall would lift the cumulative deficit since 2021 to approximately 762Moz.

Gold remains the monetary leader. Silver remains the higher-beta follower with a structurally depleted physical market.

🟠 COPPER — CONSOLIDATING NEAR HISTORIC LEVELS

Copper is easing modestly around $6.57/lb after reaching record territory in August.

Strong US data and higher-rate expectations are near-term headwinds, but Beijing’s new capital support for major state banks and insurers is marginally positive for Chinese credit and investment.

The larger copper story remains unchanged: constrained mine supply, inadequate project development and accelerating demand from grids, electrification, data centres and AI infrastructure.

☢️ URANIUM — ENERGY SECURITY RISK INTENSIFIES

August closed with uranium at approximately $89.68/lb in the spot market and $96.50/lb under long-term contracts.

A new report warns that Russian and Russian-controlled uranium mining capacity could rise from almost one-quarter of major global capacity in 2024 to 36% by 2040 if planned projects proceed.

That is an unacceptable strategic dependency for the West, and another argument for higher incentive prices, long-term utility contracting and accelerated development of secure Western uranium projects.

THE READ

Today’s stronger-rates trade is creating pressure across the metals complex. But Japan has delivered the day’s most important message:

Paper reserves are spent. Gold reserves reprice.

Gold remains the monetary leader. Silver provides leverage. Copper and uranium remain long-duration scarcity trades.

A few weeks ago, it felt like everyone on the timeline thought crypto was dead.

So I wanted to see how much money VCs were actually putting into crypto this year compared to previous cycles. It’s an interesting leading indicator.

That matters because investors aren't putting up that kind of money unless they expect a decent ROI. They can be wrong, but billions still being deployed is a useful counterpoint to the idea that crypto is dead.

• Deals per month are down 56% from 2022
• Seed rounds per month are down roughly 77%

Basically, no more spraying and praying. They're writing huge checks to a handful of proven companies (Kalshi, Polymarket, stablecoin rails) and being much more selective about everything else.

The upside to this is we're seeing a new generation of dApps with no VC money behind them.

That means no VC allocations waiting to unlock, or VC funds waiting to dump on you at TGE. 

This is much healthier compared to what we had in the past.

Bitcoin ETFs pulled in roughly $3.54B in August.
ETH ETFs attracted about $1.84B over the same month.

But what about all the other altcoin ETFs? Is there actually demand beyond the big 2?

Here’s what I found:

One interesting date is August 28th.

Bitcoin ETFs saw roughly $202M in net outflows, but several other crypto ETFs were still attracting money.

ETH took in about $102M, XRP $26M, SOL $17.3M, and HYPE $4.5M.
One day isn’t enough of a sample size, though. 

Here’s how those four non-BTC categories looked across the full trading week of August 24–28:

• $ETH: +$815.7M
• $SOL: +$142.7M
• ripple:native: +$110.5M
• $HYPE: +$56.8M

Nice, so there was demand beyond BTC and ETH.

SOL and XRP both attracted more than $100M that week, and HYPE brought in another $57M.

Those three combined took in roughly $310M, although ETH still attracted way more than all 3 put together. 

But the following week is where the picture gets more interesting.

From August 31 through September 4, net inflows into the SOL funds tracked by Farside slowed to just $4.9M. HYPE’s fell to $12.3M.

Both were still positive for the week, but the pace was very different from what we’d just seen.

And that happened while Bitcoin ETFs attracted another $987M.

So there’s clearly demand beyond BTC and ETH, but I wouldn’t call it a broader trend yet. SOL and HYPE’s inflows slowed sharply the following week, even while BTC kept attracting money.

SOL, XRP, and HYPE are the ones I’m watching. I’m more interested in whether they can keep attracting money over the next month than how much they brought in during one strong week.

2 quick thoughts

1. I'm surprised Solana hasn't been attracting more inflows from TradFi
 
2. Not too excited for any other future altcoin ETFs. I don't see how they can move the needle if these aren't.

🚨 BREAKING NEWS: HAPAG-LLOYD AND FIMI ARE PUSHING HARD FOR APPROVAL OF THE $ZIM DEAL

A new article reports that they received another 30 days to improve the offer and address the Israeli government’s concerns. The revised structure would give Israel greater control over $ZIM Israel, direct access to 16 new ships, and stronger protection of strategic shipping routes.

https://t.co/cEdugahZY3

OUR TAKE:

The stated buyout price is $35 per share, valuing $ZIM at approximately $4.2 billion. However, once you include employee compensation, the assets and part of the business being transferred to FIMI, and other expenses, Hapag-Lloyd is effectively paying around $45 per share. This means its models likely valued $ZIM at at least $60 per share when they made the offer.

And that valuation was calculated before the “golden swan” event we are now witnessing in shipping rates, which is nothing short of historic and re rating the entire industry. 

Why would Hapag-Lloyd pay so much? Because it understands that $ZIM is worth much more.

Take a pen and paper and add up all of $ZIM’s assets, cash, vessels, and long-term charter contracts. You can easily reach a sum-of-the-parts valuation of more than $100 per share.

But even that calculation understates the real value because many of these assets cannot simply be bought today, regardless of how much money you have. The average delivery time for a new container ship is more than three years, while many large LNG dual-fuel ships ordered today will not be delivered until 2029 or 2030.

Recreating $ZIM’s fleet, contracts, routes, and operating network would take years. That scarcity makes the whole company worth considerably more than the simple sum of its parts.

The original $35 bid was made when shipping rates were far lower. It is like bidding for an oil company when oil is at $60, while oil is now trading at $90.

At current rates, $ZIM will have more than $30 per share in cash by year-end, more than its entire current public market value ($28.5).

With aggressive buybacks and dividends, it is easy to see $ZIM doubling from here within the next few years while continuing to offer one of the highest dividend yields in the market.
